Add a quartic worked example, such as y = (x − 1)²(x + 2)(x − 3), because the card only works through cubics and the new point covers quartic graphs too.

confirm.reason: The bank card teaches the same factor and repeated-root ideas but only for cubics, so covering quartics (whose ends both go the same way, with quartic examples and questions) would widen its scope rather than make a small change.

draft.title: Cubic and quartic graphs
card: A factorised polynomial shows its x-intercepts. Set each bracket to zero. For y = (x + 2)(x − 1)(x − 3), the x-intercepts are x = −2, 1 and 3.
Single factor
a bracket that appears once, such as (x − 1). The graph crosses the x-axis at that point.
Squared factor
a bracket that appears twice, such as (x − 1)². The graph touches the axis and turns back without crossing.
Cubed factor
a bracket that appears three times, such as (x − 1)³. The graph flattens at the axis as it crosses.
draft.remember: Read the x-intercepts from the brackets. One factor crosses, a squared factor touches, a cubed factor flattens.

a.q: For y = (x − 4)²(x + 1), what does the graph do at x = 4?
opts: Touches the x-axis and turns back
Crosses the x-axis without flattening
Flattens as it crosses the x-axis
Does not meet the x-axis
a.why: The factor (x − 4) is squared, so x = 4 is an x-intercept where the graph touches the axis and turns. A single factor would cross. A cubed factor would flatten as it crosses.
a.clue: Look at the power on the bracket (x − 4).

b.q: A graph is y = (x + 2)(x − 3)³. What does it do at x = 3 and at x = −2?
opts: Flattens as it crosses at x = 3, crosses at x = −2
Crosses at x = 3, flattens as it crosses at x = −2
Touches and turns at x = 3, crosses at x = −2
Flattens as it crosses at both x = 3 and x = −2
b.why: The bracket (x − 3) is cubed, so the graph flattens as it crosses at x = 3. The bracket (x + 2) appears once, so the graph simply crosses at x = −2. The powers belong to the brackets, not to the numbers inside them.
b.clue: Match each power to its own bracket, then set each bracket to zero.

a.best: Touches the x-axis and turns back

b.best: Flattens as it crosses at x = 3, crosses at x = −2

final.title: Cubic and quartic graphs
card: A factorised polynomial shows its x-intercepts. Set each bracket to zero. For \(y = (x + 2)(x - 1)(x - 3)\), the x-intercepts are \(x = -2\), \(x = 1\) and \(x = 3\).
Single factor
a bracket that appears once, such as \((x - 1)\). The graph crosses the x-axis at that point.
Squared factor
a bracket that appears twice, such as \((x - 1)^{2}\). The graph touches the axis at a turning point, without crossing.
Cubed factor
a bracket that appears three times, such as \((x - 1)^{3}\). The graph crosses the axis at a stationary point of inflection.

1.alt: The cubic \(y = (x + 2)(x - 1)(x - 3)\). It crosses the x-axis at \(x = -2\), \(x = 1\) and \(x = 3\), one crossing for each single factor.

3.alt: The cubic \(y = (x + 2)(x - 1)^{2}\). At \(x = 1\), from the squared factor \((x - 1)^{2}\), the graph touches the x-axis at a turning point and turns back without crossing. At \(x = -2\), a single factor, it crosses.

final.remember: Read the x-intercepts from the brackets. One factor crosses, a squared factor touches at a turning point, a cubed factor crosses at a point of inflection.

a.q: For \(y = (x - 4)^{2}(x + 1)\), what does the graph do at \(x = 4\)?
opts: Touches the x-axis at a turning point
Crosses the x-axis with no stationary point
Crosses the x-axis at a point of inflection
Does not meet the x-axis
a.why: The factor \((x - 4)\) is squared, so \(x = 4\) is an x-intercept where the graph touches the axis at a turning point. A single factor would cross. A cubed factor would cross at a stationary point of inflection.
a.clue: Look at the power on the bracket \((x - 4)\).

b.q: A graph is \(y = (x + 2)(x - 3)^{3}\). What does it do at \(x = 3\) and at \(x = -2\)?
opts: Point of inflection at \(x = 3\), crosses at \(x = -2\)
Crosses at \(x = 3\), point of inflection at \(x = -2\)
Turning point at \(x = 3\), crosses at \(x = -2\)
Points of inflection at both \(x = 3\) and \(x = -2\)
b.why: The bracket \((x - 3)\) is cubed, so the graph crosses at \(x = 3\) with a stationary point of inflection. The bracket \((x + 2)\) appears once, so the graph simply crosses at \(x = -2\). The powers belong to the brackets, not to the numbers inside them.
b.clue: Match each power to its own bracket, then set each bracket to zero.
